```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# Render from the project root so these relative paths work
pby     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_permanova_by_year.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pooled  <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_permanova_pooled.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
envfit  <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_pcoa_envfit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gapy    <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_models_by_year.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
gapp    <- read_csv("outputs/tables/genus_gap_model_pooled.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cp1g    <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp1_genera_at_hi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
est     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_estimates.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fitted  <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_fitted.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cp_st   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp_composition_stations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  summarise(m = mean(pct), .by = c(year, impact, cp))

pool_all <- pooled |> filter(genera == "all genera")
yr  <- pool_all |> filter(term == "year_f")
ixn <- pool_all |> filter(term == "impact:year_f")
gpool <- function(trm, tr = "sqrt") gapp |> filter(transform == tr, term == trm)
e_  <- function(prefix) est[startsWith(est$parameter, prefix), ]
cpv <- function(y, g, k) cp_st$m[cp_st$year == y & cp_st$impact == g & cp_st$cp == k]
fp  <- function(g, y) 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == g & fitted$year == y]
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
```

## Why nematodes?

- The 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout released oil that reached the deep seafloor
- Nematodes dominate deep sea sediment, live their whole lives in the mud, and reproduce quickly
- Earlier work suggests they can recover faster than many other sediment animals
- That makes them a good group in which to look for early signs of recovery

::: notes
About one minute. Keep this short. The point is that nematodes are a reasonable group in which to expect early recovery, but it is an expectation we want to check against data.
:::

## Our question

**Between 2010 and 2011, did nematode communities at oil impacted stations become more similar to those at unimpacted stations?**

- Working hypothesis: heavily and moderately impacted stations move toward the controls
- "Recovered" means within the normal range of variation among controls, not identical to a control
- Original plan was a simulation out to 2022; two sampling years cannot support that, so we changed course after feedback from Kevin Shoemaker

::: notes
Explain that two healthy sites are never identical, so recovery has to be measured against how different the controls are from each other. Mention the change of plan briefly and honestly.
:::

## The data

- Nine stations: 3 heavily impacted (HI), 3 moderately impacted (MI), 3 unimpacted controls (NI)
- Sampled in 2010 and 2011, two sediment layers each (0 to 1 cm and 1 to 3 cm)
- Nematodes counted and identified to genus (a handful of animals only to family were set aside)
- Four sediment measurements per station and year: aluminum (Al), barium (Ba), PAH44, and total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH)
- Each year analysed on its own, with its own controls; layers averaged, so 9 stations per year
- 2010 values are percentages and 2011 values are counts, so we compare composition, not abundance

::: notes
Mention that the layers come from the same spot, so they are not independent. Genus lists differ between years partly because of naming and identification detail, which is one reason each year is analysed separately; the one analysis that compares years was repeated on only the genera found in both. The six animals without a genus were all at one station in 2011. All cleaning decisions are logged in the supplement.
:::

## Putting a number on "how different"

Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between two communities:

$$
BC_{ij} = \frac{\sum_k |y_{ik} - y_{jk}|}{\sum_k (y_{ik} + y_{jk})}
$$

- $y_{ik}$ is the square root of the percentage of genus $k$ at station $i$ in a given year
- 0 means the same mix of genera, 1 means no genera in common
- Calculated separately for 2010 and 2011, then drawn as a two dimensional map (NMDS)

::: notes
Square root transformation stops a few very common genera from dominating. We repeated every analysis on untransformed data as a check and say where the two disagree.
:::

## Communities separate by impact within each year

![](outputs/figures/genus_nmds_by_year.png){fig-align="center" height="390"}

Genus level maps, one per year, so the axes differ between panels. Within a year, stations of the same impact level sit near each other.

::: notes
Each year is its own analysis, so positions cannot be compared across the two panels. Whether communities changed between years is tested separately, on the PERMANOVA slide.
:::

## Are the patterns more than chance? (PERMANOVA)

```{r permanova}
bind_rows(
  pby |> filter(transform == "sqrt", model == "impact", term == "Model") |>
    transmute(Test = paste("Impact level,", year), `R squared` = R2, p = `Pr(>F)`),
  yr  |> transmute(Test = "Year (both years)", `R squared` = R2, p = `Pr(>F)`),
  ixn |> transmute(Test = "Impact x year (both years)", `R squared` = R2, p = `Pr(>F)`)
) |>
  mutate(p = fmt_p(p)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

- Impact level separates communities clearly in 2011 and borderline in 2010 (the 2010 result depends on the transformation)
- Communities changed between years, but the change did not clearly differ by impact level, and that is the term most relevant to recovery
- Three stations per group means low power

::: notes
Explain PERMANOVA as shuffling labels and asking how often a shuffle separates the communities as well as the real labels. Per year we shuffle whole stations. For the two year test, year and impact x year are tested by shuffling years within stations, because impact never changes within a station.
:::

## Does sediment chemistry line up with the communities?

![](outputs/figures/genus_pcoa_env.png){fig-align="center" height="360"}

- PCoA of the Bray-Curtis distances, with Al, Ba, PAH44 and TPH fitted as arrows
- Ba, PAH44 and TPH line up with the community axes in both years (R squared `r sprintf("%.2f", min(envfit$r2[envfit$variable != "Al"]))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(envfit$r2[envfit$variable != "Al"]))`); Al does not
- Impact class and the hydrocarbon gradient overlap so much that nine stations cannot separate them

::: notes
The hydrocarbon variables load together on one PCA axis, so they act as a single gradient. Entering impact level and the two environmental PCs together in one PERMANOVA left nothing significant on its own, with only four residual degrees of freedom, so we treat that as exploratory. The environmental values also differ a lot between years at the control stations, so the PCA is done within each year.
:::

## Distance to the controls

![](outputs/figures/genus_gap_by_year.png){fig-align="center" height="360"}

- Gap = average dissimilarity to the three controls minus how different the controls are from each other (zero = as close as controls are to each other)
- Every impacted station had a larger gap in 2011; HI gap grew about `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$estimate)` per year (95% interval `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0")$upper)`)
- With untransformed data the estimate is `r sprintf("%.2f", gpool("year0", "raw")$estimate)` and the interval includes zero

::: notes
A mixed model within each year, with station as a random effect and the two layers as repeated measures, then one model for both years. Report the number carefully: the direction is the same in both versions and none points toward recovery, but the size of the increase depends on the transformation. So we say we found no evidence of moving closer. Twelve observations per year, six stations.
:::

## What kind of nematode differs? Colonizers

![](outputs/figures/cp_composition.png){fig-align="center" height="300"}

- Each genus has a colonizer-persister (c-p) score: 1 = fast reproducing and disturbance tolerant, 5 = slow reproducing and sensitive
- Colonizer (c-p 1) animals: about `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "HI", 1))`% of HI communities in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "HI", 1))`% in 2011, against `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "NI", 1))`% and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "NI", 1))`% at controls
- About `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * cp1g$share_of_cp1_at_HI[1])`% of the colonizers at HI stations are one genus, *`r cp1g$genus[1]`*, so the pattern rests largely on one organism

::: notes
This is the clearest difference we found, and it fits the idea from our proposal that opportunists increase where disturbance is strong. Say plainly that it came from looking at the data, so it is exploratory, and that it rests mostly on one genus and not a gradual shift across the whole community. Every HI station had more colonizers than every NI station in both years.
:::

## A model for the colonizer share

Colonizer animals $y_{st}$ out of $n_{st}$ at station $s$ in year $t$:

$$
y_{st} \sim \text{BetaBinomial}(n_{st}, p_{st}, \kappa)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}(p_{st}) ={} & a + b_{HI} HI_s + b_{MI} MI_s \\
& + (c + d_{HI} HI_s + d_{MI} MI_s)(t - 2010)
\end{aligned}
$$

- Likelihood written by hand, fitted with `optim`, profile likelihood intervals
- Beta binomial beats a plain binomial (stations vary more than counting error)
- $d_{HI}$ asks whether the HI change differs from the NI change

::: notes
Beta binomial lets each station's true proportion vary around the group mean, with kappa controlling that extra variation. The key parameter is d_HI. If heavily impacted stations were converging on controls, their colonizer share would fall relative to controls and d_HI would be negative. 2010 sample sizes are reconstructed from percentages, and the result did not change when we halved or doubled them.
:::

## Colonizer model result

![](outputs/figures/colonizer_fit.png){fig-align="center" height="330"}

- 2010: odds of a colonizer about `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$odds_ratio)` times higher at HI than NI (95% interval `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_upper)`)
- NI fell from about `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("NI", 2010))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("NI", 2011))`%; HI stayed near `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("HI", 2010))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", fp("HI", 2011))`%
- $d_{HI}$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$estimate)` (profile interval `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$profile_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$profile_upper)`): the gap widened

::: notes
The gap widened because the controls dropped, not because colonizers increased at heavily impacted stations. That is the opposite of convergence, so no evidence of recovery in the colonizer share by 2011. We cannot say why the controls changed. Profile likelihood plot is on the next slide.
:::

## Profile likelihoods for the colonizer model

![](outputs/figures/colonizer_profiles.png){fig-align="center" height="420"}

The 95% interval is where the curve lies below the dashed line. Left: HI minus NI in 2010. Right: difference in yearly change.

## What we can and cannot say

- **Supported:** impacted and unimpacted stations hosted different communities in both years, with more colonizers where impact was heavy
- **Not supported:** recovery by 2011; but one year is a short time, so this does not show recovery is absent
- **Limits:**
  - The controls shifted as much as the impacted stations, which could be a real regional change or a difference in sampling or identification between years
  - Three stations per group, no pre spill baseline, and impact is partly tangled with location
  - 2010 sample sizes are reconstructed

::: notes
Be upfront that the shared shift between years is the main limitation. Two years of data cannot separate a real regional change from a methods change.
:::

## Where this goes next

- Questions about the dataset: were sampling and identification the same in both years, and were hydrocarbons and metals measured the same way (the control values differ a lot between years)?
- Do later surveys exist (for example 2023)? That would allow a recovery rate to be estimated and tested against a prediction
- Compare *Halomonhystera* and the other differing families with published responses to oil
